title: Review: The Nineteenth Century
subtitle: History, happiness, freedom and faith: the century that tried to finish philosophy and broke it open instead
objectives: By the end you will be able to place the major thinkers of Days 59–67 on a single map of nineteenth-century thought
Compare how Hegel, Marx, Schopenhauer and Nietzsche understood the direction (or pointlessness) of history
Contrast the utilitarian answer to 'How should I live?' with the answers of Kierkegaard, Nietzsche and the pragmatists
Explain how Mill, Kierkegaard and Nietzsche each defended the individual against the crowd, and how their reasons differed
Identify the problems the nineteenth century handed on to the twentieth
hook:
Berlin, 1820. A sharp-tongued thirty-two-year-old named Arthur Schopenhauer has just been given permission to lecture at the university. He has one demand: his lectures must be scheduled at exactly the same hour as those of the most famous philosopher in Germany, G.W.F. Hegel, whom he considers a windbag. The result is a humiliation. Hegel's hall is packed; Schopenhauer's is nearly empty, and his course soon fizzles out.

That little scene captures the nineteenth century. It opened with Hegel's dream of a single grand system in which reason would understand the whole of history. It closed with that dream in pieces: Schopenhauer saw only blind striving, Kierkegaard insisted that no system could live your life for you, Marx said philosophy should change the world rather than interpret it, Nietzsche declared God dead, and the American pragmatists asked what difference any of it made in practice. Meanwhile Bentham and Mill tried to put ethics on a scientific footing. Today we step back and look at the whole century together, grouping our nine lessons around the questions they shared.

sections.heading: The Big Picture: Philosophy After Kant
sections.body:
Remember where we left off on Day 58. Kant had argued that the mind actively structures experience, that we can know things only as they appear to us (phenomena) and never as they are in themselves (noumena), and that morality rests on reason alone. Almost every thinker this unit is responding, directly or indirectly, to that achievement and its loose ends.

Three forces shaped their responses. The first was **history**. The French Revolution and Napoleon had shown that the social world could be torn down and rebuilt within a single lifetime, so philosophers began to ask whether ideas, values and even reason itself have a history. The second was **industry**. Factories, railways and huge new cities created both astonishing wealth and appalling poverty, and with them new questions about work, class and the purpose of government. The third was **science**, above all Darwin's *Origin of Species* (1859), which suggested that human beings were animals shaped by natural processes rather than specially created.

You can sort the century's thinkers by how they handled these forces:

- **System builders**: Hegel tried to show that history is reason unfolding; Marx turned that story into an account of economic struggle.
- **Reformers**: Bentham and Mill wanted to measure laws and actions by their effects on human happiness, and to protect individual liberty.
- **Rebels of the individual**: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche attacked systems, crowds and comfortable morality in the name of the single, passionate, choosing person.
- **Pessimist**: Schopenhauer saw the world as an expression of blind, insatiable Will and looked for escape rather than progress.
- **Experimenters**: Peirce, James and Dewey brought philosophy down to earth, judging ideas by their consequences in experience.

These are rough labels, and every thinker resists his box. But they help us see the debate as a conversation rather than a list.

sections.heading: How They Answered the Same Question: Is History Going Anywhere?
sections.body:
For **Hegel** (Day 59), history is the story of **Geist**, Spirit or Mind, coming to know itself and become free. Its engine is **dialectic**: every position, pushed far enough, reveals internal contradictions that force a new, richer position which preserves what was true in the old one. (Recall that the tidy formula "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" is mostly a later popularization; Hegel rarely used those words.) In the master-slave dialectic, the master who seems to win turns out to depend on the slave, while the slave, through work, comes to recognize his own power. In Hegel's lectures on world history, freedom grows from one person (the despot), to some (the Greek and Roman citizens), to all. Yet philosophy can only understand an age after it has matured: the owl of Minerva, he wrote, spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk.

**Marx** (Day 63) kept Hegel's dialectic but, as he put it, set it back on its feet. History is driven not by ideas but by material conditions: who owns the means of production and who must sell their labor. This is **historical materialism**. The economic base shapes the superstructure of law, religion and philosophy, and every society so far has been a theater of class struggle. Under capitalism, workers suffer **alienation** from the product of their work, from the activity of working, from their own human nature and from one another. Marx predicted that capitalism's contradictions would produce revolution and eventually a classless society. Where Hegel's owl arrives at dusk, Marx's eleventh thesis on Feuerbach demands action: the philosophers have only interpreted the world; the point is to change it.

**Schopenhauer** (Day 60) rejected the whole idea of progress. Beneath the world as **representation** lies the world as **Will**, a blind, purposeless striving that drives everything from gravity to sexual desire. Because we are expressions of Will, we are condemned to oscillate between the pain of wanting and the boredom of having. History is just the same story in different costumes. The only relief lies in turning Will against itself: in the absorbed contemplation of art, especially music; in compassion, which sees that all suffering beings are one; and, for the rare saint, in ascetic renunciation, an idea he found echoed in Hindu and Buddhist thought.

**Nietzsche** (Days 65–66), who began as Schopenhauer's disciple, rejected both Hegel's optimism and Schopenhauer's resignation. History has no built-in goal; values have a messy **genealogy**, rising from the struggle between master and slave moralities. The death of God threatens **nihilism**. His answer is not a new law of history but a new attitude: to affirm life so fully that one could will its **eternal recurrence**.

The pragmatists offer a quieter fifth answer. Dewey (Day 67) kept Hegel's sense of growth but dropped any grand destination: progress is something people achieve piece by piece, by solving problems intelligently together.

sections.heading: How They Answered the Same Question: How Should I Live?
sections.body:
**Bentham** (Day 61) offered the clearest answer of the century. His *Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation* (1789) opens: "Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure." The right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number, the **greatest happiness principle**. He even proposed a hedonic calculus to measure pleasures by intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fruitfulness, purity and extent. This is **consequentialism**: only outcomes matter.

**Mill** (Days 61–62) defended Bentham's principle but refined it, distinguishing higher pleasures of the intellect and imagination from lower bodily ones: "It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied." The classic objections remain: utilitarianism seems to permit sacrificing an innocent person when the numbers add up, and it is hard to see how happiness could ever be measured precisely.

Notice how different this is from Kant (Day 56). For Kant, consequences are irrelevant to an action's moral worth; what matters is duty and the form of your maxim. Bentham and Mill invert that completely.

**Kierkegaard** (Day 64) found both approaches beside the point. Ethics as a set of universal rules or calculations misses the individual who must actually choose, in anxiety and without guarantees. He described three stages of existence: the **aesthetic** (living for pleasure and novelty, ending in boredom and despair), the **ethical** (commitment, duty, marriage), and the **religious**, reached only through a passionate **leap of faith** like Abraham's. Truth, he said, is subjectivity: what matters is not the objective content of a belief but how one lives it.

**Nietzsche** went further still. Utilitarian "happiness" was for him the ideal of the herd and the last man; he joked that man does not strive for happiness, only the Englishman does. His alternative is an ethic of excellence and self-overcoming: create your own values, express your **will to power** in mastery of yourself, and practice amor fati.

**James** (Day 67) offered a bridge. Like the utilitarians he cared about consequences; like Kierkegaard he believed some choices must be made with our whole passional nature, without waiting for proof. His "will to believe" applies to genuine options that are living, forced and momentous.

So the century bequeathed at least four live answers: maximize well-being, commit yourself passionately, create and affirm, or experiment and see. Day 83's applied ethics and Day 85's revival of virtue will show all of them still in play.

sections.heading: The Individual Against the Crowd
sections.body:
One theme unites thinkers who otherwise agreed on almost nothing: fear of conformity in an age of mass society.

**Mill**'s *On Liberty* (1859), written with deep influence from **Harriet Taylor Mill**, warned against the **tyranny of the majority**, not only through laws but through the social pressure of public opinion. His answer was the **harm principle**: the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. Over himself, Mill wrote, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign. He defended near-total freedom of thought and discussion because even false opinions keep true ones alive. In *The Subjection of Women* (1869) he applied the same logic to marriage and politics, arguing that the subordination of women was a relic that held back all of humanity.

**Kierkegaard** attacked "the crowd" from a religious angle. In an essay titled "The Crowd Is Untruth" he argued that in a crowd no one takes responsibility. The press, the public and the comfortable state church all let people avoid the terrifying task of becoming a self before God.

**Nietzsche** called the crowd "the herd" and saw modern democratic and Christian morality as herd instinct dressed up as virtue. Unlike Mill, he had no interest in equal rights; his concern was that mass culture would crush the rare individuals capable of greatness.

And from America, **Emerson**'s "Self-Reliance" (Day 67) insisted that whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist.

Compare their reasons. Mill defends individuality because it serves human progress and happiness, which keeps him a utilitarian. Kierkegaard defends it because each soul stands alone before God. Nietzsche defends it for the sake of excellence, and openly rejects equality. Marx is the great dissenter: for him the isolated individual of liberal theory is itself a product of capitalism, and real freedom can be achieved only collectively.

sections.heading: God, Suffering and Meaning
sections.body:
The nineteenth century is when religious doubt went mainstream among intellectuals, and each of our thinkers responded differently.

- **Hegel** treated Christianity as a picture-language for truths that philosophy expresses in concepts: God is Spirit coming to know itself through history.
- **Schopenhauer** was an atheist who nevertheless admired the ascetic saints of Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism for their insight that life is suffering.
- **Marx** called religion "the opium of the people," in a passage that also describes it as the sigh of the oppressed creature and the heart of a heartless world: a painkiller for real misery whose causes are economic.
- **Kierkegaard** fiercely defended faith but insisted it was a paradox, not a conclusion of reason, and attacked the comfortable Danish church as a betrayal of Christianity.
- **Nietzsche** announced the death of God as a cultural event whose consequences Europe had not yet faced, and diagnosed Christian morality as rooted in **ressentiment**.
- **James** defended the right to religious faith as a genuine option and studied religious experience by its fruits.

One way to see the century is as a series of experiments in living after the old certainties. Schopenhauer found the world without God bleak and sought escape. Nietzsche tried to find it exhilarating. Marx tried to fill the gap with a secular hope of a just society. Kierkegaard chose the leap. James and Dewey suggested we judge beliefs by what they do for human lives.

sections.heading: What the Nineteenth Century Left Behind
sections.body:
Every movement of the next century can be traced to these thinkers. Existentialism (Days 76–79) grew from Kierkegaard and Nietzsche. Critical theory (Day 80) grew from Marx and Hegel. Modern welfare economics, cost-benefit analysis and effective altruism grew from Bentham and Mill. Freud owed debts, by his own later admission, to Schopenhauer's idea of an unconscious, irrational will. And pragmatism's experimental spirit fed into twentieth-century science and philosophy of science.

But the century also left a reaction. Around 1900, two young Cambridge philosophers, Bertrand Russell and G.E. Moore, rebelled against the Hegelian idealism then dominant in British universities. Meanwhile in Germany the mathematician Gottlob Frege was quietly inventing modern logic. They wanted philosophy to be clear, precise and rigorous, more like mathematics than like poetry or prophecy. That reaction launches our next unit: the analytic tradition, beginning tomorrow with Frege and Russell.

keyQuote.text: The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point is to change it.
keyQuote.source: Karl Marx, Theses on Feuerbach (1845), Thesis 11

modernConnection.title: One Evening Online, Seen Through Nineteenth-Century Eyes
modernConnection.body:
Picture an ordinary evening. A delivery rider finishes a shift assigned by an app, paid per drop, never meeting a manager. She gets home, scrolls a social feed for an hour, finds herself furious at strangers, buys something she did not need, and lies awake wondering what she is doing with her life.

Each of our thinkers would see something different. **Marx** would see alienation: work broken into tiny, algorithmically managed units, with the rider separated from the product, the process, her coworkers and any sense of creative control, while the platform's owners capture the value. **Bentham** would ask whether the app economy produces more total happiness than what it replaced, and want the data. **Mill** would worry about whether the platform's content moderation respects the harm principle, and whether the feed's pressure to conform is a new tyranny of the majority. **Nietzsche** would see ressentiment in the outrage and the last man in the cheap comforts. **Schopenhauer** would recognize the endless cycle of craving and boredom; psychologists now call something similar the hedonic treadmill. **Kierkegaard** would say her late-night dread is not a malfunction but anxiety, the dizziness of freedom, calling her to become a self. **Dewey** would ask how she and others could inquire together and redesign the system democratically.

The exercise shows why these thinkers remain alive: they built lenses we still use, often without knowing their names. But it also shows the limits of any one lens. Marx's analysis says little about her inner dread; Kierkegaard says little about her wages; the utilitarian sums can miss both. The nineteenth century's deepest lesson may be that human life is economic, psychological, moral and spiritual all at once, and no single system captures it, a point Kierkegaard made against Hegel and that the century as a whole ended up proving.

vocabulary.definition: Hegel's process by which a position's internal contradictions drive thought (and history) toward a richer position that preserves what was true in the earlier one.
vocabulary.example: In Hegel's master-slave dialectic, the master's apparent victory turns into dependence on the slave.

vocabulary.definition: The blind, purposeless striving that Schopenhauer held to be the inner nature of all reality, behind the world as we represent it.
vocabulary.example: For Schopenhauer, both a falling stone and a lover's longing are expressions of the Will.

vocabulary.definition: The utilitarian principle that the right action is the one that produces the greatest overall happiness (pleasure minus pain) for all affected.
vocabulary.example: A government applying the greatest happiness principle would fund the program that relieves the most suffering per dollar.

vocabulary.definition: Mill's principle that society may rightfully restrict a person's liberty only to prevent harm to others, not for the person's own good.
vocabulary.example: Under the harm principle, a law against drunk driving is justified, but a law against eating junk food at home is not.

vocabulary.definition: In Marx, the estrangement of workers under capitalism from their product, their activity, their human nature and each other.
vocabulary.example: A worker who repeats one tiny task all day, never seeing the finished product, illustrates Marx's idea of alienation.

vocabulary.definition: Kierkegaard's term for the passionate, personal commitment to the religious life that cannot be reached by reason or evidence.
vocabulary.example: For Kierkegaard, Abraham's willingness to obey God's command required a leap of faith beyond ethics.

vocabulary.definition: Nietzsche's term for the festering resentment of the weak toward the strong, which he claimed gave birth to slave morality.
vocabulary.example: Nietzsche would diagnose ressentiment in someone who condemns all success as greed because he cannot achieve it.

vocabulary.definition: Peirce's rule that our conception of anything is our conception of its conceivable practical effects.
vocabulary.example: Using the pragmatic maxim, she asked what observable difference it would make if the two theories were true.

thinkingExercise.title: The Nineteenth-Century Dinner Party
thinkingExercise.prompt: Synthesize the unit by staging an imaginary argument. Choose a real problem from today and let four of this unit's thinkers debate it. Spend 10 to 15 minutes.
steps: Choose a current issue that matters to you: for example, a four-day work week, banning phones in schools, a new religious movement, or artificial intelligence replacing jobs.

Pick four thinkers from Days 59–67, at least one from each of these groups: system builders (Hegel, Marx), reformers (Bentham, Mill), rebels (Kierkegaard, Nietzsche), and pessimist or experimenters (Schopenhauer, Peirce, James, Dewey).
Write two or three sentences in each thinker's voice giving their verdict on the issue, using at least one key term from their lesson.
Identify the deepest disagreement among them. Is it about facts, about values, or about what a human being is?
Finish with your own verdict, naming which thinker you found most persuasive and the strongest objection you would have to raise against that thinker.

summary: After Kant, nineteenth-century philosophy was shaped by revolution and history, industrialization and Darwinian science.

Hegel saw history as Spirit's dialectical progress toward freedom; Marx rooted that dialectic in class struggle and material conditions; Schopenhauer saw only blind Will; Nietzsche saw a genealogy of values and called for affirmation.
Bentham and Mill judged actions by their consequences for happiness, while Kierkegaard, Nietzsche and James insisted on passionate individual commitment that no calculation can replace.
Mill, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche and Emerson all defended the individual against the crowd, but for utilitarian, religious and aristocratic reasons respectively; Marx argued freedom must be collective.
The century's responses to religious doubt ranged from Hegel's philosophical Christianity to Marx's opium, Kierkegaard's leap, Nietzsche's death of God and James's will to believe.
Its legacies feed existentialism, critical theory, utilitarian policy and pragmatism, while the reaction against Hegelian idealism launched analytic philosophy.

quiz.question: What did Hegel mean by saying the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk?
options: Philosophy can predict the future course of history
Philosophy understands an era only after it has matured and is passing
Wisdom comes only to people in old age
Reason is powerless compared with the Will
quiz.explanation: Hegel meant philosophy comprehends a form of life only in retrospect, which is why Marx demanded a philosophy that changes the world.

quiz.question: Hegel regularly described his dialectic using the formula 'thesis, antithesis, synthesis.'
quiz.explanation: The formula is largely a later popularization; Hegel himself rarely used those terms.

quiz.question: How did Marx change Hegel's dialectic?
options: He abandoned the idea that history develops at all
He made individual faith the driving force of history
He grounded it in material and economic conditions and class struggle rather than the development of Spirit
He argued history moves in endless identical cycles
quiz.explanation: Marx said he set Hegel's dialectic back on its feet: material conditions, not ideas, drive historical change.

quiz.question: According to Schopenhauer, which of these offers temporary relief from the suffering produced by the Will?
options: The aesthetic contemplation of art, especially music
Accumulating wealth
Participating in revolutionary politics
Maximizing the greatest happiness of the greatest number
quiz.explanation: Schopenhauer held that absorption in art, above all music, along with compassion and asceticism, can quiet the Will.

quiz.question: Which statement best captures Mill's refinement of Bentham's utilitarianism?
options: Only duty, not consequences, determines right action
Pleasures differ in quality, so higher pleasures of the mind count for more than mere bodily ones
Happiness should be ignored in favor of liberty
Pleasure is an illusion produced by the Will
quiz.explanation: Mill distinguished higher and lower pleasures: better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

quiz.question: A city bans smoking in private homes where only the smoker lives, purely to protect the smoker's own health. Which principle would Mill invoke to object?
options: The pragmatic maxim
The categorical imperative
Master morality
The harm principle
quiz.explanation: The harm principle allows coercion only to prevent harm to others; over his own body and mind the individual is sovereign.

quiz.question: Harriet Taylor Mill had no influence on John Stuart Mill's thinking about liberty or the equality of women.
quiz.explanation: Mill himself credited Harriet Taylor Mill as a major influence and collaborator, especially on On Liberty and women's equality.

quiz.question: A factory worker spends every day attaching one part to a product she never sees completed, under rules she has no say in, for a wage that barely covers rent. Which concept best describes her situation?
options: Alienation
Eternal recurrence
The teleological suspension of the ethical
Fallibilism
quiz.explanation: Marx's alienation describes estrangement from the product, the activity, one's human nature and others under capitalist production.

quiz.question: In Kierkegaard's three stages of existence, which stage is characterized by living for pleasure and novelty and tends to end in boredom and despair?
options: The religious stage
The ethical stage
The aesthetic stage
The dialectical stage
quiz.explanation: The aesthetic stage is the life of pleasure and variety; its emptiness can prompt the move to the ethical.

quiz.question: Nietzsche's concept of ressentiment describes the festering resentment of the weak that he believed gave rise to slave morality.
quiz.explanation: In On the Genealogy of Morality, ressentiment is the creative force behind the slave revolt in morality.

quiz.question: Why does Nietzsche's eternal recurrence function as a test?
options: It proves mathematically that time is circular
It shows that only pleasure matters
It establishes the existence of an afterlife
It asks whether you could will your life to repeat forever, revealing whether you truly affirm it
quiz.explanation: Most scholars read it as a thought experiment testing total affirmation of life, linked to amor fati.

quiz.question: What do Kierkegaard and Nietzsche most clearly share?
options: Christian faith
Hostility to the crowd and to systems that neglect the passionate individual
Support for democratic equality
Belief that history is the progress of Spirit
quiz.explanation: Kierkegaard was a Christian and Nietzsche an atheist, but both attacked mass conformity and system-building in favor of the individual.

quiz.question: Which thinker argued that when an option is living, forced and momentous and evidence cannot decide, our passional nature may lawfully choose?
options: W.K. Clifford
Jeremy Bentham
William James
Charles Sanders Peirce
quiz.explanation: This is the argument of James's 'The Will to Believe'; Clifford held the opposite view.

quiz.question: Marx described religion as 'the opium of the people,' a painkiller for real suffering whose causes he believed were economic.
quiz.explanation: The phrase comes from his 1844 introduction to a critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, which also calls religion the sigh of the oppressed creature.

quiz.question: Which development at the end of the nineteenth century set the stage for analytic philosophy?
options: Russell and Moore's rebellion against Hegelian idealism, together with Frege's new logic
Kierkegaard's attack on the Danish church
Schopenhauer's lectures in Berlin
Dewey's founding of the Laboratory School
quiz.explanation: The reaction against idealism and the invention of modern logic launched the analytic tradition we begin on Day 69.

goDeeper.body:
Historians of philosophy often describe the nineteenth century as a struggle over Hegel's legacy. After his death in 1831 his followers split into 'Right Hegelians,' who read him as a defender of Christianity and the Prussian state, and 'Left' or 'Young Hegelians,' including Ludwig Feuerbach and the young Marx, who turned his dialectic against religion and existing institutions. Kierkegaard, who attended Schelling's lectures in Berlin in 1841–42 hoping for an alternative to Hegel, spent his career satirizing 'the System.' Karl Löwith's classic *From Hegel to Nietzsche* traces how this single inheritance produced both Marxism and existentialism.

A second, less obvious thread is the rise of the 'masters of suspicion,' a phrase coined by the French philosopher Paul Ricoeur for Marx, Nietzsche and Freud. Each taught that our conscious beliefs hide deeper forces, whether economic interests, the will to power, or unconscious drives. Schopenhauer arguably anticipated all three. Their method of looking behind what people say to what really motivates them became one of the most powerful and most disputed tools in modern thought: it can unmask hypocrisy, but if everything is suspected, the suspicious theory itself can be unmasked too.

Finally, it is worth asking who is missing from this unit's story. Harriet Taylor Mill is increasingly recognized as a philosopher in her own right. Frederick Douglass, Sojourner Truth and other abolitionists made powerful arguments about freedom and human dignity that rarely appear in philosophy syllabi. We return to some of these voices on Day 86.

readings.title: From Hegel to Nietzsche
readings.author: Karl Löwith
readings.note: A classic study of how the Hegelian system broke apart into Marx, Kierkegaard and Nietzsche.

readings.title: On Liberty
readings.author: John Stuart Mill
readings.note: Short and readable; chapter 2 on freedom of thought and discussion is essential.

readings.title: The Communist Manifesto
readings.author: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
readings.note: Brief and dramatic; read Part I for the theory of history as class struggle.

readings.title: Freud and Philosophy: An Essay on Interpretation
readings.author: Paul Ricoeur
readings.note: The source of the phrase 'masters of suspicion'; demanding but rewarding.

questions: Which nineteenth-century thinker offers the best diagnosis of our own time, and which offers the best cure? Are they the same person?
Mill, Kierkegaard and Nietzsche all defended the individual against the crowd. Does their agreement on this point matter more than their disagreements about why?
Is the 'hermeneutics of suspicion' a liberating tool or a corrosive one?
